messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn when Kwame was closing up his chair at the salon. The last client had left, and he was wiping down the mirrors, the scent of hair product and disinfectant sharp in the air. He had just stepped out the back door to take out the trash when a man emerged from the alley, reeking of cheap liquor, and pressed something hard into Kwame’s ribs. The man demanded his wallet, his phone, the cash from his tips. Kwame handed everything over, his hands shaking, his breath catching in his throat. The man shoved him against the brick wall and then was gone, leaving Kwame slumped on the cold ground, the smell of alcohol clinging to his coat.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame tried not to think about it. He told himself it was just a robbery, that he was lucky to be unharmed, and that he should just move on. He pushed the images away, but they came back anyway—mostly as vivid pictures that would flash into his mind without warning: the cracked brick pattern of the wall, the man’s unshaven jaw, the glint of streetlight on metal. Other times the memory played like a film he couldn’t stop, the whole scene replaying from the moment he heard footsteps behind him to the sound of his own keys hitting the pavement. When his wife asked what happened, he found himself unable to explain. He knew what had occurred, but the words felt trapped, as if the event existed in a place beyond language.

The real trouble began when a client corrected him. A woman in her forties, a regular, told him he had used too much product on her ends. Kwame felt his chest tighten. His hands grew clumsy, and he could not shake the feeling that she was hiding something, that her criticism was a signal of danger. The moment she left, he replayed the interaction obsessively, asking himself what he had done wrong, why he had provoked her. He began to avoid certain clients—the ones who were particular, the ones who seemed impatient—because their corrections felt like accusations. He started to believe that if he just said or did the right thing, he could prevent another attack.

Kwame’s world narrowed. He stopped going out after dark. He avoided the back alley entirely, using the front door even when it meant carrying heavy boxes around the block. When a customer walked in smelling of alcohol, he would feel the film start playing again—the shove, the cold wall—and he would excuse himself to the back room, heart pounding. He started to see threat everywhere. A man lingering by the bus stop, a stranger adjusting his jacket—each gesture seemed suspicious, a prelude to violence. He would scan the salon floor repeatedly, watching the door, watching hands, watching for anything that felt wrong. He became certain that the world was full of people waiting to hurt him, and that the only way to stay safe was to be ready, to be perfect, to never make a mistake.

His wife noticed he had grown distant. He stopped joining her for Saturday errands, claiming he was tired. At work, he turned down social invitations from the other stylists. He spent his evenings alone, replaying the robbery in his head, then scolding himself for dwelling on it, then trying even harder to push the thoughts away. The more he tried not to think about the trauma, the more it surfaced—a loop he could not escape. Each time a memory intruded, his vigilance spiked. Each time he avoided a person or a place, he felt a brief relief, followed by the creeping certainty that the next threat was already closing in.

What finally brought Kwame to a therapist was a morning in the salon when a new client, a young man with a sharp voice, asked him to redo a section of a haircut. Kwame’s hands went cold. He felt the old film start to roll. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood gripping the sink, his breath shallow, the smell of disinfectant mixing with the phantom scent of alcohol. He realized he could no longer tell the difference between a bad haircut and a danger. He made an appointment that afternoon, hoping someone could help him find the words he had lost, and terrified that the world outside his door would never feel safe again.
